title: Orcas Are Ramming Boats — And Scientists Think It's a Game
summary:
Imagine you're sailing near Spain when suddenly — BAM! — something huge hits your boat. That's what's happening to sailors off the coasts of Spain and Portugal. A small group of fewer than 50 orcas (also called killer whales) has been ramming boats since 2020. They've even sunk some!

On July 23, orcas hit a sailboat called Idem again and again until it sank. The two people on board were rescued safely. On August 29, four orcas broke half the rudder off a 42-foot yacht. Less than 48 hours later, another yacht needed a rescue escort to port.

Why are they doing this? Scientists aren't sure. One idea: the orcas are just playing. Atlantic bluefin tuna — their favorite food — are now easier to find, so young orcas have more free time. They might see boat rudders as fun toys. Another idea: young orcas are practicing hunting skills. Sailboats move fast and quiet, kind of like tuna.

"This is like a training toy," said biologist Bruno Díaz López. "It's a shame that we humans are in the middle of this game, but they are learning."
why_it_matters: It reminds us that when people change the ocean — like making it easier for orcas to find food — animals may change how they behave around our boats and us.

background_read: Orcas (also called killer whales) are actually the largest members of the dolphin family, and they live in oceans all over the world in family groups called pods.
These boat bumps are happening near Spain and Portugal (two countries in Europe that sit side by side on the Atlantic Ocean), where many sailboats travel each summer.
Atlantic bluefin tuna (a huge, fast fish that orcas love to hunt) have become easier for the whales to find, which may be why the young ones have extra time on their hands.
Article_Structure: WHO: A group of fewer than 50 orcas (killer whales) off the coasts of Spain and Portugal, plus the sailors whose boats they hit
WHAT: The orcas have been ramming boats since 2020, sinking one sailboat and breaking the rudder off a 42-foot yacht
WHERE: The waters off Spain and Portugal; the sailboat Idem sank on July 23, and another yacht needed a rescue escort to port
WHY: Scientists aren't sure, but they think the orcas may be playing or practicing hunting skills, since tuna are easier to find and rudders look like fun toys

perspectives.description: They are worried because their boats are being damaged, and a sinking boat could put people in real danger.
They think the orcas are probably just playing or practicing hunting, not trying to hurt anyone on purpose.
They find it fascinating that these smart animals are learning something new, but they also want the whales and the sailors to stay safe.
